summary: line current (Iₗiₙₑ) is what the Three phase calculator works out, and it gets there from the line voltage, the phase current (Iₚₕ), the line voltage (Vₗiₙₑ) and the apparent power. That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Three phase calculator work?
sections.html:
The Three phase calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports line current (Iₗiₙₑ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the connection type); then you type in the line voltage (Vₗiₙₑ), the phase current (Iₚₕ) (2), the line voltage (Vₗiₙₑ) (2) and the apparent power (S).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in volts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in amperes. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in volts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Three phase calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Line current (Iₗiₙₑ)=the square root of (3) × phase current (Iₚₕ)
Phase voltage (Vₚₕ)=line voltage (Vₗiₙₑ)
Line current (Iₗiₙₑ)=phase current (Iₚₕ)
Phase voltage (Vₚₕ)=(1 ÷ 3) × the square root of (3) × line voltage (Vₗiₙₑ)
Phase voltage (Vₚₕ)=(1 ÷ 3) × apparent power (S) ÷ phase current (Iₚₕ)
Power factor=active power (P) ÷ apparent power (S)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Connection type set to Delta (D) and Phase current (Iₚₕ) = 10 A. Working through the relationship above gives Line current (Iₗiₙₑ) = 17.32 A.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Line current (Iₗiₙₑ) = 17.32 A should be roughly the size you expected from Connection type set to Delta (D) and Phase current (Iₚₕ) = 10 A.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Voltage, opening in volts

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Three phase calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the line voltage, the phase current (Iₚₕ) and the line voltage (Vₗiₙₑ) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Three phase calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns line current (Iₗiₙₑ), derived from the line voltage, the phase current (Iₚₕ) and the line voltage (Vₗiₙₑ). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Three phase calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the line voltage, the phase current (Iₚₕ), the line voltage (Vₗiₙₑ) and the apparent power, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter phase current (Iₚₕ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Phase current (Iₚₕ) opens in amperes and the chip beside it offers 3 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Line current (Iₗiₙₑ) = 17.32 A. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Three phase calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
